clinicalPearls: Lunotriquetral instability arises from injury to the lunotriquetral interosseous ligament, causing ulnar-sided wrist pain and a sense of clunking.
It may occur in isolation, often after a fall on the extended, radially deviated and pronated wrist, or as part of a reverse perilunate (progressive perilunar) injury.
The Reagan ballottement test and the Kleinman shear test reproduce pain and abnormal motion at the lunotriquetral interval.
When secondary stabilisers also fail, the lunate follows the scaphoid into flexion, producing a volar intercalated segment instability (VISI) posture.
Static radiographs are often normal; a break in the smooth proximal Gilula arcs or a lunotriquetral step-off is suggestive.
Ulnar impaction syndrome frequently coexists and should be assessed, as positive ulnar variance may need addressing.
Arthroscopy is the reference standard for confirming and grading the tear when imaging is inconclusive.
reference.pathophysiology: The lunotriquetral interosseous ligament, strongest volarly, tightly couples the lunate and triquetrum within the proximal carpal row. Disruption, whether traumatic or degenerative and often associated with ulnar impaction, uncouples this linkage. With loss of the palmar lunotriquetral ligament and secondary volar stabilisers, the triquetrum extends while the lunate, still tethered to the scaphoid, is drawn into flexion, generating a VISI collapse pattern. The resulting abnormal midcarpal kinematics produce pain, clicking and reduced load tolerance on the ulnar side of the wrist.
additionalDifferentials: Extensor carpi ulnaris tendinopathy or subluxation
additionalInvestigations: PA, lateral and clenched-fist radiographs assessing Gilula arcs and carpal alignment
Lateral view to detect a VISI pattern with abnormal scaphoid flexion and capitolunate angulation
MRI or MR arthrography of the lunotriquetral ligament and TFCC
Wrist arthroscopy for definitive diagnosis and grading
redFlags: Features of a progressive perilunate injury or dislocation
Fixed VISI deformity indicating chronic complete disruption
Associated ulnar impaction with lunate or triquetral chondral change
Neurovascular compromise after a high-energy injury
reference.prognosis: Isolated partial injuries often respond to non-operative care, whereas complete or chronic instability may require repair, reconstruction or lunotriquetral arthrodesis, with outcomes influenced by coexisting ulnar impaction.
pitfalls: Overlooking associated ulnar impaction and treating the ligament in isolation.
Interpreting normal static radiographs as excluding instability.
Missing a reverse perilunate injury pattern.
Confusing lunotriquetral instability with a primary TFCC tear.
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
management: Treat isolated partial or acute injuries non-operatively with wrist splinting, activity modification, hand therapy and a corticosteroid injection into the lunotriquetral interval
Address coexisting ulnar impaction, including an ulnar shortening osteotomy or wafer procedure for positive ulnar variance
Confirm and grade the instability with MR arthrography and wrist arthroscopy when the diagnosis is unclear or symptoms persist
Offer ligament repair or reconstruction for complete or symptomatic chronic instability without fixed deformity
Perform lunotriquetral arthrodesis for refractory or chronic instability, particularly when a VISI deformity is established
Rehabilitate with hand therapy after intervention and refer to a hand and wrist surgeon for persistent ulnar-sided pain or clunking
